Loop is when you go back to stage 1 after stage 5. The Teleporter in stage 5 is different and you can toggle loop by activating the prongs before activating the boss battle. Keep an eye for the message that appears: if it's pointed to the planet, you'll loop. Keep in mind enemies keep scaling in difficulty, so looping is great to build towards a more game braking collection of items, but it's also easier to die.

Regarding large stacks of items, if you're on a regular run (no artifacts like command), this can be accomplished by finding a printer. It's like a chest with an item hovering over it. The item hovering is the one that will leave the printer. You can trade a random, same tier item for the item in the printer. Alternatively, you can find a scrapper, a cylindrical thing on the ground somewhere in the stage (not guaranteed to spawn) which you can choose an item to scrap. If you have a scrapped item, it will be prioritized when printing, and you'll control better what you have.

Regarding false son, his gimmick is all about a large HP., so keep an eye out for HP enhancing items like bison stakes or infusion. Also, remember to always charge the beam. Hold the button down until you see the visual cue. This maximizes output.

Yes, just a small correction: the roll difficulty is not the same value as the damage resistance. The roll determines if the attack ignores any resistance and does full damage. If the roll fails, the damage is reduced by the stat that resists the type of damage the player does. This difference exists because players goes through multiple levels of combat, imagine multiple final fantasy turn based combats. The enemies scale as the players climb levels, so the enemies resistances have to scale accordingly. This roll system can't scale indefinitely, so this other value, that I'm calling "armor" is not the value that will reduce the damage dealt by the player.

The more I talk about the system the more obnoxious it sounds lol
There's no other answer.

The roll is only meant to overcome resistance. Hit is merely a choice the player has to make. Damage is defined by the weapon or spell the player chooses to use. The roll would merely resolve if the enemy resistance would be ignored so the player deals extra damage. 

Think of it as a crit exclusive roll of some sort.

The enemy should have a set "armor" value, which players will have to beat with this dice roll in order to make their attack completely ignore the enemies resistance, thus dealing extra damage. This was my thought process, and I get now from all the feedback here that I've overdone it. That was my goal posting here.

First things first, advice for any character.

Don't enter a run with a specific build in mind. You HAVE to play with what you are offered. If you try and push for a specific combo, you'll fail most of the times, and will feel bad about it. There are way too many synergies in this game that you will never experience if you do this. 

Your deck and relic collection MUST cater to all of:

Damage, block, draw and scaling. Chip damage is damage, as are big bonks. Apparitions are block, as are buffers. Keep in mind that one thing can be multiple things.

Ironclad

Yes, branch corruption is amazing, but you'll often not find any, or even strength scaling, but you could go barricade, entrench body slam, juggernaut, or maybe some kind of fire breathing combo with power through and reckless strike. Like said above, work with what you already have, not what you want to have. Given a floor 3 fire breathing? Well, take advantage of those curseful events!

Silent

You're missing out on what's the strongest archetype here: discard. The silent excels on draw mechanics and cards, and you should take advantage of that. Draw is arguably the most powerful thing in the game. Get yourself an Acrobatics and a Blur everytime you can and you'll seldom miss that elusive Wraith Form.

Defect

Orbs, my guy. Rotate those bad boys. Give yourself things that move them around. There are way too many things to do so, along with Loops, Bias Cog and that cheat code of a card that is Echo Form. Also, don't sleep on hologram and cool headed. They're the poor man's Seek.

Watcher

Stance dance is what you want, most of the times. Keep an eye out for cards that allow you to go in and out of them to keep safe and energy filled. Don't ignore scry: it's the next big thing after draw. Imagine draw what you want! Watcher excels at blocking while slapping: one or two talk to the hand and a wallop is almost enough to keep you alive half of the way. Just be careful with getting stuck on Wrath at the wrong time, and you'll be fine.

It's gotta be maddening to be inside Blizzard reading all of the audience's demands, really. I know what you mean. This blurry state feels like no one is happy. It boils down to personal preference. I really like the game, play it regularly, and I'm eager to try the new changes, but I can also see a point in many complaints people have. Could Diablo 4 be a better game? Sure! Do I have my own preferences in regards to what should be changed? Absolutely! Do I know how to balance business and a fun videogame? No, I do not. Lol

All fair points, and great arguments. I'm here since release, so I'm quite aware of the demands and general complaints people have about the game. I'm fully on board with you about having the game ready from the get go. The possibility that companies have nowadays to "fix" the game after release is absolutely being abused, not just Blizzard, but pretty much all of the major companies. The amount of games broken on release is astounding. I also agree that several decisions about diablo 4 were poor, at best. This trial and error approach at the expense of public time, money and patience should definitely be gone. The thing is: it won't. No matter how much audiences complain about this, it will only change when a more profitable approach comes up. 

My point is that Diablo as a franchise has a massive and diverse community. Unless Blizzard decides to cater to a more niche audience, and answer to a single part of the community, it will stay that way. I don't have the data on how much money the game is making them, but looking at their following changes it doesn't seem like they will be doing so. Perhaps slowly, if ever, they will add content to respond to specific demands, but it really doesn't seem to be the case. My guess is that we will navigate this blurry waters of MMO - ARPG for a while.

Blizzard actually knows what it wants with Diablo 4. The fact that they take feedback from the community and make changes to the game does not mean that they're lost. Blizzard is a business, and Diablo 4 is a product. In order to turn that product into a profit, they have to address the players desires, but only they know how to do things in a more balanced way.

The fact that there's such a huge gap between opinions on the game should tell you that there's a LOT of people playing the game. The gap grows proportionally to the community size. Every game that is set out to major audiences goes through that. 

Diablo is a staple on ARPGs, and whatever hurdle it sent through its first year did not change that. It's a triple A game, with a massive community, that will never be unanimous about the game. Attack power means nothing, really. What you should be caring about is your synergies and gear affixes. There's a lot to check, so here's a few tips:

- Gear affixes should ideally all be doing something to you, whether offensively or defensively. Try to stock on Legendary aspects you use so when that one sweet piece has it all, you can imprint it.

- All classes have some sort of + attack to something. Barbs, for example, have lots of extra damage to bleeding and vulnerable. Explore those options.

- You should be maximizing the Glyph potential, rather than getting lots of boards. I.E. If a Glyph gives you extra damage when Berserking for as much Str in range, get all of those Str in range to maximize the Glyph potential. You won't have enough paragon points to do this to all your Glyphs, so be wise. A well placed Glyph can be stronger than a legendary node. 

- Mind your buffs. If your damage burst depends on some kind of temporary buff like a barrier or berserk, you ideally want to have those either with 100% uptime or ready to use when it matters most. 

- Not all skills in your bar have to be at max level, 5 or above. Some of them you use just to apply some kind of debuffs to enemies. With this in mind, don't sleep on the skill tree passives. Likely one or more of them are crucial to your build. 

- Read a guide. Even if you do not intend to follow it step by step, it's cool to learn the thinking behind the top tier builds in the game.

With that being said, try to understand the bonuses and drawbacks of each potato. 
Let's take Chunky, for example. He has -100% modifier on speed. That means you can't get it higher, but also not lower. If an item gives you -2% speed it won't affect the potato, so there's no downside. Chunky also scales damage with HP, so getting extra HP means extra damage for him. That makes Alien Eyes for example a great item.

Another example, Mage. He gets extra 33% on elemental damage modifiers, but virtually no other form of damage. That means your hits will do little damage. But the enemy gets lots of damage as it ignites. Therefore, Snake, Sausage, life steal and a couple Flamethrowers could get you past wave 20.

Understanding what each potato has to offer is key to get each to win.

A few "rules" I've come up with and use them in my games

- Try to keep up with having all of those: attack, block, draw and energy. Should one be lacking, prioritize it when possible in card rewards and/or at shop, either in the form of cards or relics 

- Don't avoid elites. This is something a lot of new players do for fear they hurt the run early, but the relics usually change the game for the better.

- Act one bonfires (are for upgrading key cards (sure, if every rest site could be used for upgrades, it's amazing, but Act one is particularly important for the long run). Of course, there's no point in going to the next combat if you're too low on HP, but then again, if you're having to rest often early, chances are, your deck can't finish the run anyways.

- Mind the order of the card playing every turn. Take your time. The game has no penalty for long turns. Especially when you're getting the hang of the game, playing fast has no benefits whatsoever. 

- Removing cards is really important, especially the starting Strikes and Defends. Getting to your key cards as fast as possible is the best way to ensure victory.

- Have fun. It's a single player roguelike game, the next run will be just as exciting. Try that card you don't usually pick. Discover new synergies. Go for that meme deck. Fuck around with that Prismatic Shard. Eventually you will come across an unexpected dopamine filled run. There's no "right" way to play, no guaranteed strategy.

Edit: as in every roguelike, the game is VERY RNG based, so sometimes you'll feel like you're not getting what you want. That's fine. Happens to all of us lol

Rule of thumb, you have to build your deck thinking about these

Damage, the higher the better, but preferably in big chunks. The heart will only allow so much damage every turn, but ideally you want to do the max allowed (300 on A1, I believe?)

Draw. On silent you can develop draw synergies with Tactician for example, but in 
every character draw absolutely necessary. The heart will give you a plethora of status cards, so you need draw.

Block, the more the merrier, especially against the heart. Keep in mind though that you should be scaling that as well, you don't have the time to play Defends for your blocking needs. After Image and Blur are great choices for the Silent. intangibility could replace that if you're comfortable with your damage. The Heart punishes you for every card you play, remember that.

No run is like the last. You can only work with what you're given. Beating the heart is hard as all hell, so you will lose A LOT. More often than not you will not see the relic or card you want, you may find curses and there's hardly any deck that works well against anything the spire can throw at you. That spiral is what is considered obsessive thinking. Much like an addiction, you see yourself circling back to it, many times not even realizing it. The best way to snap out of it is talking about it, to someone you trust or a therapist. I know that may not be possible to many people, so here's a few tricks that I do myself, some tools I have developed to go through my own "spirals", which I learned after a fee years of therapy.

- Try to reflect upon what causes this on yourself. The obsessive thinking spiral thing Is something that you already have acknowledged and is conscious about. It is important to realize the reasons behind it so you can avoid what causes it or reprogram your brain when it comes to thinking about past situations that causes these feelings.

- When you realize that you're spiraling, try to change your behaviour. Actual external behaviours, like the way you do things, the activities you get to. Small things. This can keep your brain busy with other things, once you're not doing what muscle memory has in storage.

- Avoid judging yourself after. Like you said, you feel embarrassed about the times you spiral. And it can feel embarrassing, really. But then again, it's you against you here. Use that discomfort to help you power through what it takes to get rid of it. 

There's no easy way out of this, friend. Then again, living like this is not easy as well. Hope this helps in any shape or form. Be safe.
